title: Thirty-three hours, and two lines
learning_goal: Know that the longest single leg of the chapter — the whole length of Italy — is two lines in the notebook, and that we cannot say which stations he passed.

narration.script: Twenty past seven, Friday morning, Turin. Four o'clock, Saturday afternoon, Brindisi. Almost thirty-three hours — the whole length of Italy. The notebook gives it two lines. We know the railway reached the heel in 1865. Which stations he stopped at, nobody has told us.

media.note: 2088x1679 — the whole harbour from above the town: the inner basin, the moles, a steamer at anchor. Establishes the port before M-245 goes close. Slot 1/2.

media.note: 2095x1525 — the landing station at the harbour: rails and a train on the quay, sheds, a steamer alongside with smoke up. Exactly the moment the chapter ends on. Slot 2/2.

overlays.text: Turin 7:20 am Friday → Brindisi 4:00 pm Saturday · ≈ 33 hours
Rails reached Brindisi in 1865 — which is why the port could be the port

production_notes: SEGMENT 8, first third (45 s; the segment's ceiling is 205 words and this scene spends 44). THE HONEST THINNESS IS THE POINT: the fact sheet cannot name a single station between Turin and the heel (its Gaps list forbids using the later Peninsular Express stop list), so the guide says so out loud rather than padding — 'which stations he stopped at, nobody has told us'. That sentence is also the chapter's argument in miniature. NO anachronisms: no wagons-lits, no dining car; those belong to the 1890s and Fogg sat up all night in a compartment.

review.notes: Scene Developer + Narrator draft 2026-08-27. SLOT TIMINGS, and the sentence each is timed against: 0-24 M-246 (the harbour, wide) — 'Twenty past seven, Friday morning, Turin… the whole length of Italy.'; 24-45 M-245 (the landing station, rails and a steamer) — 'The notebook gives it two lines. We know the rails reached the heel in 1865…' Two timed captions in 45 s against a ceiling of four. Both engravings are 1899, i.e. 27 years after Fogg — the captions state facts about 1865 and 1872 and never date the pictures to his day.
